Selfiecide

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
BUT FIRST, let me take a selfie. The last words often said before a selfie goes wrong. Diagnosed as a disease and banned in India - what is selfiecide and how are we dealing with it in SA?

Summary:
Selfiecide An accidental death that has been caused whilst trying to take a dangerous Selfie pic.

The term selfie was word of the year in the Oxford dictionary in 2013. "A photograph that one has taken of oneself, typically one taken with a smartphone or webcam and shared via social media." But the "selfie craze" has since grown and has since been classed as a mental disorder - by the American psychiatric Association in 2014.
APA said there are three levels of the disorder:

Borderline selfitis : taking photos of one’s self at least three times a day but not posting them on social media
Acute selfitis: taking photos of one’s self at least three times a day and posting each of the photos on social media
Chronic selfitis: Uncontrollable urge to take photos of one’s self round the clock and posting the photos on social media more than six times a day.

Although these are international examples (see below) - we do have some local examples - and we are going to spend the morning with the labstore ladies - a group of young woman between 19-23 whose job it is to take selfies in the social media company -Lab store. The are self proclaimed addicts and talk about the dangerous behaviour extreme selfie taking leads to, but also about the culture of selfie taking; in which, young impressionable ladies are "allogroomed" to include selfies in their daily lives. Nadia Scheepers and Abigail Ferns will talk about the stresses of selfie culture and how sometimes they take 50 selfies just to get the perfect one to post on social media - they will talk about the self editing process. Our teens are serious about taking selfies, so serious that it has become, for some, more important than living - and if the selfie response is less than expected or there is negative backlash or a photo is trolled - suicide is often considered as a final resort. Nadia is called the "Selfie queen."

Further information:
https://theconversation.com/the-deadly-selfie-game-the-thrill-to-end-all-thrills-59266?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Latest%20from%20The%20Conversation%20for%20May%2017%202016%20-%204874&utm_content=Latest%20from%20The%20Conversation%20for%20May%2017%202016%20-%204874+CID_ed49aeb00d7287923b771b8ab9b09ab4&utm_source=campaign_monitor_africa&utm_term=The%20deadly%20selfie%20game%20%20the%20thrill%20to%20end%20all%20thrills


Taking a selfie every now and then isn't going to kill you, or will it? Since the term was officially coined there have been a confirmed 49 fatalities world wide attributed to Selfie taking, (the selfie is not the cause of death but is taken just before a tragic event). There is a new, more dangerous selfie craze which has been popularized on social media since the beginning of 2016 (especially on snapchat and instagram) - called the "Extreme Selfie's." This is where someone does something potentially dangerous and takes a selfie during the process - for example a 15 year old teenage boy in India died when taking a selfie while posing with his fathers gun - 39 calibre pistrol and accidentally shot himself. But he is not the first one - there are several cases of this - please see pictures. World wide there are many cases: 1. Jenni Rivera - Selfie taken by Mexican singer Jenni Rivera (right) and her crew while flying a plane - moments before the aeroplane crashed in December 2012.
2. Reggaeton singer Jadiel (real name Ramon Alberto González Adam), who took a selfie while driving his motorbike at the same time, he did not see a truck, and died. Rochester, New York.
3. Xenia Ignatyeva, who in April 2014 climbed a high bridge to impress her friends, but then slipped and fell and was electrocuted when she grabbed live cables. Her beautiful young face looks flushed as she stares into the camera, exhilarated and energised. 4. Image of a police officer taking a selfie with a man who jumped from a bridge in Ankara, Turkey, in 2014. 5. This selfie was nicknamed the "ultimate selfie" - because Ben Innes - a British hostage on the Egypt Air flight MS181 that was hijacked by Sief Eldin Mustafa - took a selfie with the hijakcer and posted is on twitter. More examples: http://viralscape.com/stupid-selfies-that-got-people-arrested/


Taking dangerous selfie's - which may cause ones death - selfiecide have been banned in India - where 40% of the selfie-caused deaths have occurred. Amanda Du Preez has studied this as a cultural phenomenon and can add elements to the mental phenomenon and talk about the effects psychologically.

Pam Lourenco is a "selfie specific" social media expert - recommended to me by Sarah Britten (who is on maternity leave), Pam has a very good sense of humour, understand that this is also part of the "Darwin awards" and can explain how this phenomenon has bloomed into something dangerous, where one can get help and be counselled and the signs parents can look out for, but also how to curb "selfie taking" and make your teen understand the consequences of being addicted to selfies.

Selfiecide or Selfiesteem?
It’s a dangerous trend that’s already resulted in at least 50 documented deaths and it seems to be getting ever more ridiculous. Why are people risking their safety and lives just to capture what they hope will be the ultimate selfie? Carte Blanche explores addiction to selfie-taking - now classified as a psychiatric disorder.

The ussie... the healthie... and even the belfie ... It’s the evolution of the selfie... and on to more dangerous trends like the Kylie Jenner big lip challenge, the sellotape selfie AND this year’s extreme selfie challenge – snap the pic while flirting with danger.
Pam: “It feeds into our narcisssim, that you are seen as someone who is daring, and that’s the message that they want to portray.”

findings Derek: “It’s crazy, maybe a little pathetic that we’re sitting here in 2016 talking about dangerous pictures?
Amanda: “If your whole exsistence starts depending on those likes, I do think you are a little bit in trouble.”

Nadia: “This generation, my generation, and younger mostly use it as like something to build their self-esteem.”

Show photos Derek: “You’re known as the selfie queen?
Nadia: “Apparently (laughs shyly)…. because I’m on snapchat a lot, so when a person snaps me a picture, I have to take a picture back.”

[NATS SOUND girls walking and laughing… ]
Shots from their websites. Taffy Muzuwa, the marketing team’s self-titled “creative nerd” explains why 30 percent of all photos posted to social media are selfies.
Taffy intv Taffy: “I think it’s a place to showcase your beauty in a way, to get other people to see you, because a selfie, is not a selfie until it’s posted up.”
Shots from her website and singing Nathi Mavumengwana uses instagram and snapchat to market her singing talent and love of music.
Nathi intv Nathi: “I just believe that if someone likes something, they will follow you, and if they don’t, they don’t. For me its not about how many followers, for me its more the quality than the quantity.”
[Upsound singing…(see website promoting music)]
What she’s seeing with selfie’s – telfie trends explained Nadia: “Selfies have taken over everything. Like before, you could go out to places, and just enjoy yourself, but now it’s like you have to take a picture in order to remember the fun times you had.”
Derek: “What are the trends?”
Nadia: “What used to be really popular was the duck face.
Derek: “You do that quite well. A lot of practice.”
Nadia: “Now there’s the filters, especially on snap chat, especially the dog filter.”
Taffy intv explains selfie taking Taffy: “Twist, get the pout going with the eyes the ‘smi-eyes’.”
Derek: “So it’s a skill?”
Taffy: “Yes it is.”
India: 40% of selfie-related deaths Globally there have been 49 confirmed deaths from risky selfies, the majority in India – where they are now banned. And, after a 17 year old fell to her death while pursuing an extreme selfie, Russia sent out a safety pamphlet
Amanda: “Selfie sticks are prohibited, because it is a danger. People no longer look at the ground, they look at the camera or at the screen.”
Taffy: “It’s like that risk, are you not afraid that something’s going to happen to you. Just for a moment, where people are going to see it and they’re going to like it. It’s not worth it.”
EgyptAir Hostage Situation pictures In March, during a hostage situation on Egypt Air, British hostage Ben Innes asked an air hostess to snap his picture with hijacker Seif Eldin Mustafa, who was wearing a bomb belt. Seif was later found mentally unstable. Though Ben didn’t even snap the controversial shot himself, social media tagged it as “The Ultimate Selfie”.
Fake And in June a video surfaced of a distracted driver moments before an accident. Although it’s authenticity hasn’t been verified.
Could this be an example of a new trend – faking something likely to prove popular? #fakie
Taffy’s little sister – youg girls Taffy says many school girls market themselves online.
Taffy intv Taffy: “Obviously if you’re going to make friends its based on what you look like, how many followers you have, what do your pictures look like, whats your personality like coming out from your profile.”
Pam intv Pam Laurenco: “It’s teaching the youth, A. to be very narcissistic and very inward looking, and number 2. It’s hammering their self-esteem.”
Pam into – and self editing Social media expert Pam Laurenco says constant “self editing” can become dangerously addictive.
Pam intv


Pam: “For instance, if an 18 year old takes a photograph and her photo only gets 2 likes, and her best friend gets a photograph and it gets 50 likes, that makes her feel inadequate.”
Nathi obsession Nathi: “It can become an obsession, for other people, taking a selfie is not just taking a selfie, its like I need to get some kind of reference from people, comments and opinions, and the more people comment, its like what I believe of myself.”
Derek link LINK: Well it may be bizarre, but some people are taking selfie’s seriously – Selfitis – has been classed as a disorder by the American Psychiatric Association.
GRAPHIC BY ROBIN on screen:
Borderline selfitis: taking photos of one’s self at least three times a day but not posting them on social media
Acute selfitis: taking photos of one’s self at least three times a day and posting each of the photos on social media
Chronic selfitis: Uncontrollable urge to take photos of one’s self round the clock and posting the photos on social media more than six times a day. So-called selfitis ranges from Borderline to Chronic where you’re taking more than 6 selfies a day, all day, and posting them all on social media.



Pam Laurenco – Social Media Selfie Expert Pam says the need for social recognition is called allogrooming.
Pam allogrooming explanation Pam: “We are social animals so if you post something that we like, we will like it, we will share it, we will validate you as a social person.”
Amanda: “The rate at which people upload selfie’s, it’s a constant uploading, it’s a process, so it’s almost living in two worlds, the real and the virtual, at the same time.”
Parents and schools should monitor children’s social media and limit their followers.
Pam on schools Pam: “What schools can do is that they can educate people about what is a bad selfie, and what is crossing the line to sexual exploitation for instance.”
Amanda: “I do think that the selfie is leading us into that whole process of another self, a virtual self.”
Taffy on dangerous challenge Derek: “Now where’s the selfie going?
Nadia: “There’s no limits when it comes to selfies, It’s like you will literally take a selfie for anything to prove you did something, otherwise people wont believe you, if you don’t have a selfie to back you up.”

Pam intv Pam: “For instance, if an 18 year old takes a photograph and her photo only gets 2 likes, and her best friend gets a photograph and it gets 50 likes, that makes her feel inadequate.” Nathi obsession Nathi: “It can become an obsession, for other people, taking a selfie is not just taking a selfie, its like I need to get some kind of reference from people, comments and opinions, and the more people comment, its like what I believe of myself.” Derek link LINK: Well it may be bizarre, but some people are taking selfie’s seriously – Selfitis – has been classed as a disorder by the American Psychiatric Association. So-called selfitis ranges from Borderline to Chronic where you’re taking more than 6 selfies a day, all day, and posting them all on social media. Pam Laurenco – Social Media Selfie Expert Pam says the need for social recognition is called allogrooming. Pam allogrooming explanation Pam: “We are social animals so if you post something that we like, we will like it, we will share it, we will validate you as a social person.” Amanda: “The rate at which people upload selfie’s, it’s a constant uploading, it’s a process, so it’s almost living in two worlds, the real and the virtual, at the same time.” Parents and schools should monitor children’s social media and limit their followers. Pam on schools Pam: “What schools can do is that they can educate people about what is a bad selfie, and what is crossing the line to sexual exploitation for instance.” Amanda: “I do think that the selfie is leading us into that whole process of another self, a virtual self.” Taffy on dangerous challenge Derek: “Now where’s the selfie going? metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): BUT FIRST, let me take a selfie. The last words often said before a selfie goes wrong. Diagnosed as a disease and banned in India - what is selfiecide and how are we dealing with it in SA?
metadata.Summary: Selfiecide An accidental death that has been caused whilst trying to take a dangerous Selfie pic. The term selfie was word of the year in the Oxford dictionary in 2013. "A photograph that one has taken of oneself, typically one taken with a smartphone or webcam and shared via social media." But the "selfie craze" has since grown and has since been classed as a mental disorder - by the American psychiatric Association in 2014. APA said there are three levels of the disorder: Borderline selfitis : taking photos of one’s self at least three times a day but not posting them on social media Acute selfitis: taking photos of one’s self at least three times a day and posting each of the photos on social media Chronic selfitis: Uncontrollable urge to take photos of one’s self round the clock and posting the photos on social media more than six times a day. Although these are international examples (see below) - we do have some local examples - and we are going to spend the morning with the labstore ladies - a group of young woman between 19-23 whose job it is to take selfies in the social media company -Lab store. The are self proclaimed addicts and talk about the dangerous behaviour extreme selfie taking leads to, but also about the culture of selfie taking; in which, young impressionable ladies are "allogroomed" to include selfies in their daily lives. Nadia Scheepers and Abigail Ferns will talk about the stresses of selfie culture and how sometimes they take 50 selfies just to get the perfect one to post on social media - they will talk about the self editing process. Our teens are serious about taking selfies, so serious that it has become, for some, more important than living - and if the selfie response is less than expected or there is negative backlash or a photo is trolled - suicide is often considered as a final resort. Nadia is called the "Selfie queen."
metadata.Further information: https://theconversation.com/the-deadly-selfie-game-the-thrill-to-end-all-thrills-59266?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Latest%20from%20The%20Conversation%20for%20May%2017%202016%20-%204874&utm_content=Latest%20from%20The%20Conversation%20for%20May%2017%202016%20-%204874+CID_ed49aeb00d7287923b771b8ab9b09ab4&utm_source=campaign_monitor_africa&utm_term=The%20deadly%20selfie%20game%20%20the%20thrill%20to%20end%20all%20thrills Taking a selfie every now and then isn't going to kill you, or will it? Since the term was officially coined there have been a confirmed 49 fatalities world wide attributed to Selfie taking, (the selfie is not the cause of death but is taken just before a tragic event). There is a new, more dangerous selfie craze which has been popularized on social media since the beginning of 2016 (especially on snapchat and instagram) - called the "Extreme Selfie's." This is where someone does something potentially dangerous and takes a selfie during the process - for example a 15 year old teenage boy in India died when taking a selfie while posing with his fathers gun - 39 calibre pistrol and accidentally shot himself. But he is not the first one - there are several cases of this - please see pictures. World wide there are many cases: 1. Jenni Rivera - Selfie taken by Mexican singer Jenni Rivera (right) and her crew while flying a plane - moments before the aeroplane crashed in December 2012. 2. Reggaeton singer Jadiel (real name Ramon Alberto González Adam), who took a selfie while driving his motorbike at the same time, he did not see a truck, and died. Rochester, New York. 3. Xenia Ignatyeva, who in April 2014 climbed a high bridge to impress her friends, but then slipped and fell and was electrocuted when she grabbed live cables. Her beautiful young face looks flushed as she stares into the camera, exhilarated and energised. 4. Image of a police officer taking a selfie with a man who jumped from a bridge in Ankara, Turkey, in 2014. 5. This selfie was nicknamed the "ultimate selfie" - because Ben Innes - a British hostage on the Egypt Air flight MS181 that was hijacked by Sief Eldin Mustafa - took a selfie with the hijakcer and posted is on twitter. More examples: http://viralscape.com/stupid-selfies-that-got-people-arrested/ Taking dangerous selfie's - which may cause ones death - selfiecide have been banned in India - where 40% of the selfie-caused deaths have occurred. Amanda Du Preez has studied this as a cultural phenomenon and can add elements to the mental phenomenon and talk about the effects psychologically. Pam Lourenco is a "selfie specific" social media expert - recommended to me by Sarah Britten (who is on maternity leave), Pam has a very good sense of humour, understand that this is also part of the "Darwin awards" and can explain how this phenomenon has bloomed into something dangerous, where one can get help and be counselled and the signs parents can look out for, but also how to curb "selfie taking" and make your teen understand the consequences of being addicted to selfies.
